system: You are analyzing chronological observations from a real-world video. Identify physical object interactions using only visible evidence. Distinguish objects resting on surfaces from objects held by a person. Do not infer pickup solely from an object disappearing, changing screen position, or leaving the field of view. Do not infer manipulation solely from camera movement. Do not assume visually similar objects are the same physical instance without supporting evidence. If object identity, state transition, or temporal order is unclear, report uncertainty. Reference only supplied frame aliases. Do not invent exact event timestamps. Do not use prior knowledge of the recording or an expected answer. Return only structured JSON, without markdown or extra text.
task: Examine the chronological observations. First describe visible physical states for a small number of relevant objects, grounding each state in supplied frame aliases. Identify objects from visible appearance and keep descriptions consistent across observations only when identity is supported. Use ON_SURFACE for an object visibly resting on a surface, HELD_BY_PERSON for an object visibly supported or grasped by a person, OTHER for another observed state, and UNKNOWN when the state cannot be established. State uncertainty explicitly. Focus on visible support and hand-object relations rather than screen displacement. Absence from an image is not proof of absence from the scene. Then, only if the recorded states support a transition of the same object, optionally propose a PICKUP (surface support to held) or PLACEMENT (held to surface support) hypothesis. Cite earlier and later frame aliases that also occur in that object's state observations; use exactly its observation object description. Do not force an event, infer one from camera motion or disappearance, or invent exact timestamps. Set status EVENTS only for one or more proposed hypotheses; otherwise use UNCERTAIN for insufficient evidence or NO_CONFIRMED_EVENT for a clearly observed no-event sequence in these sampled observations. Sparse images do not establish exhaustive continuous coverage. List observations before any event hypotheses. Do not describe every visible object. Return only JSON with the supplied schema, no markdown or extra text.
